[[File:Hershaft and rivlin.jpg|upright|thumbnail|Alex Hershaft meeting with Israel's president [[Reuven Rivlin]] during a speaking tour in May 2015]]

'''Alex Hershaft''' (born 1 July 1934) is an American [[Holocaust survivors|Holocaust survivor]],<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last=Dolsten |first=Josefin |title=Holocaust survivor likens treatment of livestock to Shoah |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/holocaust-survivor-likens-treatment-of-livestock-to-shoah/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=[[The Times of Israel]] |language=en-US |issn=0040-7909}}</ref> and co-founder and president of the [[Farm Animal Rights Movement]] (FARM),<ref name="Henderson 1985">{{Cite web |last=Henderson |first=Greg |title=Alex Hershaft, president of the Farm Animal Reform Movement,... |publisher=UPI |date=March 20, 1985 |url=http://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/03/20/Alex-Hershaft-president-of-the-Farm-Animal-Reform-Movement/3600480142800/ |access-date=October 26, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Slesin 1994">{{Cite web |last=Slesin |first=Suzanne |title=Kids Who Say, 'Ugh, Cow!' |website=The New York Times |date=July 13, 1994 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/13/garden/kids-who-say-ugh-cow.html |access-date=October 26, 2016}}</ref> the [[United States]]' oldest (1976) organization devoted exclusively to promoting the rights of animals not to be raised for food.<ref name="Meatless Monday: FARM Looks at 40">{{Cite web |date=2016-10-03 |title=Meatless Monday: FARM Looks at 40 |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/meatless-monday-farm-look_b_12267028 |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=HuffPost |language=en}}</ref> Previously, he has had a 30-year career in materials science and [[environmental consulting]] and a role in movements for [[religious freedom]] and [[environmental quality]].<ref name="Gatenby">{{Cite web |last=Gatenby |first=Alex |date=2017-05-23 |title=Vegan Holocaust survivor wants to end the oppression of animals |url=https://www.standard.co.uk/lifestyle/vegan-holocaust-survivor-says-the-reason-he-survived-was-to-end-the-oppression-of-animals-a3543956.html?fbclid=IwAR1oHaz1x4n-XXr-Jvmvw_l5y4tbxuul_ym2qEYQVh9SUISkD0FURR4F7kg |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=The Standard |language=en}}</ref>

==Family and early life==
Hershaft was born in [[Warsaw]], Poland, on July 1, 1934, to fairly assimilated Jewish parents Jozef and Sabina Herszaft.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Isaacs |first=Anna |date=2015-10-02 |title=Q&A: Animal Rights Activist and Holocaust Survivor Alex Hershaft |url=https://momentmag.com/qa-animal-rights-activist-and-holocaust-survivor-alex-hershaft/?srsltid=AfmBOorXv1b8QPKEQ8xcu09N7cW96pEz-WbuP35PSg_6XdZyy7PGHkY- |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=Moment Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> Sabina was a mathematician. Jozef was a chemist researching the properties of [[heavy water]] (used as a coolant for nuclear reactors) at [[University of Warsaw]] with his colleague [[Jozef Rotblat]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=18mZrDujOm0|title=Alex Hershaft: From the Warsaw Ghetto to the Fight for Animal Rights|date=September 9, 2014|via=YouTube}}</ref>

Their research was in great demand, as Western scientists began to recognize the potential of harnessing [[nuclear technology|nuclear energy]], and both received visas to continue their work in the U.K. and the U.S. Rotblat left for the U.K just before Hitler invaded Poland in 1939 and eventually received the 1995 Nobel Peace Prize for his subsequent opposition to nuclear weapons.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=A JEWISH TELEGRAPH NEWSPAPER |url=https://www.jewishtelegraph.com/prof_401.html |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=www.jewishtelegraph.com}}</ref> Herszaft insisted on visas for his wife and young son, but those came too late.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-05-03 |title=US animal rights movement founder, Holocaust survivor in Israel for speaking tour |url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/us-animal-rights-movement-founder-holocaust-survivor-in-israel-for-speaking-tour-400948 |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=[[The Jerusalem Post]] |language=en |issn=0792-822X}}</ref>

During the war, the family was forced to move into the [[Warsaw Ghetto]], with Sabina's parents, across the street from the infamous [[Pawiak prison]]. As the Nazis began exterminating the Ghetto in late 1942, sending inmates to the [[Treblinka extermination camp|Treblinka]] death camp, all three were able to escape to the Christian side and remain in hiding.<ref>[[Norm Phelps]]. ''The Longest Struggle''. Lantern Books, 2004; p. 225</ref><ref name="articles.baltimoresun">[https://www.baltimoresun.com/1996/11/24/holocaust-survivor-heads-animal-rights-group-alex-hershaft-throws-himself-into-cause/ "Holocaust survivor heads animal rights group Alex Hershaft throws himself into cause"]  ''Baltimore Sun''. Retrieved 2014-3-4.</ref> Sabina and Alex were liberated by the allies in the spring of 1945. After the war and five years in an Italian refugee camp, Sabina emigrated to Israel, while 16-year-old Alexander arrived in the U.S. in January 1951. Sabina died in Israel in 1996.

==Research and consulting career==
Hershaft received his B.A. in 1955 from the [[University of Connecticut]], where he was active in the student senate, the school newspaper, and the soccer team. He went on to study polymer chemistry at the [[Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute]]. He gained his Ph.D. in inorganic chemistry in 1961 from [[Iowa State University]], where he was employed by the [[Ames Laboratory]] of the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]].

Hershaft began his science career at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, where he taught graduate classes in [[X-ray crystallography]]. He then spent a year running the chemistry department at the Israel Institute for Scientific Translations in Jerusalem. Upon returning to the United States in 1963, Hershaft analyzed naval operations for the [[Center for Naval Analyses]] in Arlington, Virginia.

In 1967, Hershaft joined the [[Grumman]] Aerospace Corporation in Bethpage, New York, to review potential areas of new business in air and water pollution control, and solid waste management. In 1969, one year before the first [[Earth Day]], he launched, then managed the Environmental Technology Seminar, a regional forum for study and discussion of tri-state (New York–New Jersey–Delaware) environmental issues.

In 1972, Hershaft moved to the Washington, D.C., area. He joined the consulting firm [[Booz Allen Hamilton]] in Bethesda, Maryland, to evaluate water management alternatives, impacts of electric power plants and transmission lines, and costs and benefit of data from the Earth Resources Technology Satellite.

Hershaft spent a couple more years directing environmental studies for the U.S. [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] and U.S. [[Council on Environmental Quality]] with two erstwhile consulting firms: Enviro Control and Interstate Electronics Corporation.

Between 1977 and 1981, Hershaft served as a senior scientist with the [[Mitre Corporation]] in [[McLean, Virginia]]. He studied emissions from various heating fuels and prepared protocols for assessing and cleaning up [[Hazardous waste in the United States|hazardous waste sites]] as part of the U.S. [[Superfund]] program.

==Social justice career==
Hershaft had been involved in student extracurricular activities throughout his undergraduate and graduate studies. At the [[University of Connecticut]], he served on both the Student Senate and the Campus newspaper.

In November 1961, while working at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]], Hershaft staged a major demonstration in Tel-Aviv, leading to the formation of the League for Abolition of Religious Coercion in Israel, a massive movement seeking to end repression of secular, Reform, and Conservative Judaism, as well as mixed marriages, by entrenched Orthodox authorities.<ref>''Haaretz''. November 21, 1961. Page 1.</ref>

Two years later, he turned over leadership to [[Uzzi Ornan]] and his other Israeli deputies, as he returned to the U.S. to seek support for the organization. Following the upheaval of the [[1967 Six-Day War]], the cause of religious freedom in Israel was taken up by the [[Ratz (political party)|Citizen Rights Party (Ratz)]] (now [[Meretz-Yachad|Meretz]]).
[[File:Alex Hershaft.2015.JPG|250px|thumbnail|Alex Hershaft at [[Tel Aviv University]] in May 2015]]
Between 1965 and 1978, Hershaft served on the board of the [[American Humanist Association]] (AHA), a national organization that affirms the ability and responsibility of human beings to lead ethical and fulfilling lives without reference to a supernatural being.

{{quote box
| title = 
| quote = "Most people are neither good nor evil. They are simply puppets of their capricious social norms. Nazi norms decreed that a German with two Jewish grandparents got to live, but one with three Jewish grandparents must die. Our norms decree that a dog gets to live, but a pig must die.""
| source = — Alex Hershaft <br>October 2, 2015.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Isaacs |first1=Anna |title=Q&A: Animal Rights Activist and Holocaust Survivor Alex Hershaft |url=https://momentmag.com/qa-animal-rights-activist-and-holocaust-survivor-alex-hershaft/?srsltid=AfmBOoonApV7ufQTKPBnLRlcP1ETg9ZMUP8Fj2JMTVXVbl9osSOvIqIW |website=Moment Magazine|date=October 2, 2015 }}</ref>

| fontsize = 100%

| title_bg = #f0f0ff

In 1961, shortly after arriving in Israel, Hershaft dropped meat from his diet. In August 1975, he became involved in the vegetarian movement after attending the [[International Vegetarian Union|World Vegetarian Congress]] in [[Orono, Maine]], and meeting [[H. Jay Dinshah|Jay Dinshah]].<ref name="articles.baltimoresun" /><ref>Lawrence & Susan Finsen. ''The Animal Rights Movement in America''. Twayne Publishers, 1994; p. 75.</ref><ref>Norm Phelps. ''The Longest Struggle''. Lantern Books, 2004; pp. 190, 222.</ref><ref>[http://www.vegparadise.com/24carrot411.html "24 Carrot Award"] ''Vegetarians in Paradise''. Retrieved 2014-3-4.</ref>  He reports that Robin Hur<ref>[https://www.amazon.com/Food-Reform-Our-Desperate-Need/dp/0913206059/ref=la_B001KMSBCQ_1_1 Food Reform: Our Desperate Need, by Robin Hur, PhD, 1975]</ref> (then of [[Harvard Business School]] in Boston) persuaded him in 1981, after 20 years as a vegetarian, to become vegan.
[[File:Alex hershaft seminar.jpg|thumb|Alex Hershaft addressing the 2015 [[Animal Rights National Conference]] in Washington]]
In 1976, Hershaft founded the Vegetarian Information Service (VIS) to distribute information on the benefits of a vegetarian diet. That same year, he participated in hearings before the [[Senate Select Committee on Nutrition and Human Needs]], which led to the publication of [[Dietary Goals for the United States]], and eventually to the periodic publication of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans. Subsequently, he testified before Congress in favor of the 1978 National Consumer Nutrition Information Act and the Federal Meat Inspection Act of 1978.

During that period, Hershaft also organized several conferences on strategies for promoting vegetarianism. Some participants, influenced by Peter Singer's 1975 treatise ''[[Animal Liberation (book)|Animal Liberation]]'', felt that the scope of these conferences should be expanded to include discussions of [[animal rights]].<ref>Norm Phelps. ''The Longest Struggle''. Lantern Books, 2004; p. 222.</ref>

[[File:Vegan Camp-Out main audience-19b.jpg|thumb|Alex Hershaft addressing the annual [[Vegan Camp Out]] in England in 2019]]

Accordingly, in the summer of 1981, Hershaft organized Action For Life, a national conference at [[Cedar Crest College]] in [[Allentown, Pennsylvania]], that effectively launched the U.S. animal rights movement. Participants included such animal rights pioneers as [[Cleveland Amory]], [[Ingrid Newkirk]], [[Alex Pacheco (activist)|Alex Pacheco]], [[Peter Singer]], [[Henry Spira]], [[Gretchen Wyler]], as well as radio host [[Thom Hartmann]]. These conferences continued for seven more years in San Francisco (1982), Montclair, New Jersey (1983), Los Angeles (1985), Chicago (1986), Cambridge, Massachusetts (1987), and Washington (1984 and 1991).<ref>Lawrence & Susan Finsen. ''The Animal Rights Movement in America''. Twayne Publishers, 1994; p. 76</ref><ref>Norm Phelps. ''The Longest Struggle''. Lantern Books, 2004; p. 223.</ref>

Immediately following the 1981 conference, Hershaft founded the Farm Animal Rights Movement (FARM) to promote a [[vegan]] lifestyle and [[animal rights]].<ref>Lawrence & Susan Finsen. ''The Animal Rights Movement in America''. Twayne Publishers, 1994; p. 84.</ref>

As FARM president, Hershaft launched World Farm Animals Day in 1983, Great American Meatout in 1985, Veal Ban Campaign in 1986, Letters from FARM in 1996, and 10 Billion Lives in 2011.<ref name="Meatless Monday: FARM Looks at 40"/><ref name="Gatenby"/>

In 1997, Hershaft launched a second round of 20 Animal Rights National Conferences that attracted 1500 participants and rallied and inspired the US animal rights movement each year.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kritz |first=Fran |date=2020-09-02 |title=The Warsaw Ghetto Can Teach The World How To Beat Back An Outbreak |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2020/09/02/908732924/the-warsaw-ghetto-can-teach-the-world-how-to-beat-back-an-outbreak |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

In 2015, Hershaft began reflecting on the many parallels between the Holocaust and the mass slaughter of animals for food, particularly the size and efficiency of the operations, the respective personnel structures, the surrounding secrecy, the use of cattle cars to transport victims, the cruelties preceding death,<ref name=":0" /> and the arbitrary respective social norms that induce ordinary people to perpetrate or enable extraordinary atrocities.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pfefferman |first=Naomi |date=2012-10-10 |title=Comparing animal rights and the Holocaust |url=https://jewishjournal.com/mobile_20111212/108867/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=Jewish Journal |language=en-US}}</ref> He conducted speaking tours of Israel, Germany, Poland, England, and the US. Some of the talks appear on YouTube. A book and a documentary are in the works.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-11-05 |title=The Monopolization of the Meat Industry |url=https://honeysucklemag.com/farmers-and-activists-unite-against-the-monopolization-of-the-meat-industry/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=Honeysuckle Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

In 2020, Hershaft relinquished the day-to-day operation of FARM to executive director Eric Lindstrom but stayed on as an active president.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Valentine |first=Katie |date=2020-07-27 |title=Eric Lindstrom Takes Over as Executive Director for Farm Animal Rights Movement |url=https://ladyfreethinker.org/eric-lindstrom-takes-over-as-executive-director-for-farm-animal-rights-movement/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=Lady Freethinker |language=en-US}}</ref>
[[File:Hershaft blocking a truck.jpg|thumb|Alex Hershaft blocking  a truck from entering the Smithfield, Virginia, slaughterhouse in 2005]]

Hershaft has written several hundred letters to newspaper editors about the merits of a vegan diet.<ref>https://jvs.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2012/03/JVS-Mag-No.145-June-2003.pdf

The Jewish Vegetarian</ref> He has been featured in several news reports and feature articles.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lehmkuhl |first=Vance |date=2017-04-24 |title=FARM founder speaks out on the 'unspeakable' |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/blogs/v-for-vegan/FARM-founder-speaks-out-on-the-unspeakable-.html |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=inquirer |language=en}}</ref> At the animal rights national conferences, he lectured on personal growth, leadership, social change, campaign strategies, and movement building.<ref name=":0" /><ref>Lawrence & Susan Finsen. ''The Animal Rights Movement in America''. Twayne Publishers, 1994; p. 121.</ref><ref>Norm Phelps. ''The Longest Struggle''.  Lantern Books, 2004; p. 226</ref><ref>[https://business.time.com/2012/03/22/the-meatless-and-less-meat-revolution/ "The Meatless (and Less Meat) Revolution"] ''Time''. Retrieved 2014-3-4.</ref><ref name="vegnews">[http://vegnews.com/articles/page.do?pageId=4331&catId=2 "The Brains Behind the Great American Meatout"] ''VegNews''. Retrieved 2014-3-4.</ref><ref>http://www.jewishveg.com/about-us{{Dead link|date=October 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

== Honors ==
Hershaft has been listed in Marquis' ''[[Who’s Who in America]]'', ''[[American Men and Women of Science]]'', and other biographical directories.<ref>[http://arconference.org/hall-of-fame.htm "U.S. Animal Rights Hall of Fame"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140311015517/http://arconference.org/hall-of-fame.htm|date=2014-03-11}}, Animal Rights National Conference, Retrieved October 27, 2016</ref> He has been inducted into both the U.S. Vegetarian Hall of Fame (1998) and the U.S. [[Animal Rights Hall of Fame]] (2001).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vegetarian Hall of Fame |url=https://navs-online.org/purposes-programs/hall-of-fame/ |website=North American Vegetarian Society}}</ref>

Between 1984 and 2000, Hershaft served on the governing council of the [[International Vegetarian Union]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schwartz |first=Richard H. |title=The Blogs: B'tay-Avon (Hearty Appetite) Tips for Vegetarian Living |url=https://blogs.timesofisrael.com/btay-avon-hearty-appetite-tips-for-vegetarian-living/ |access-date=2025-04-22 |website=blogs.timesofisrael.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Between 2001 and 2009, he served on the board of [[In Defense of Animals]], a national animal rights organization based in [[San Rafael, California]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barwick |first=Emily Moran |date=2016-02-03 |title=Holocaust Survivors Speak: Lessons From The Death Camps |url=https://bitesizevegan.org/holocaust-survivors-speak-lessons-from-the-death-camps/ |access-date=2025-04-22 |website=Bite Size Vegan |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Hershaft met Eugenie (Genia) Krystal while working at the Israel Institute for Scientific Translations, and they were married in Jerusalem in 1962. They were divorced in 1979. 
Their daughter, Monica Larissa Hershaft, was born in 1966.<ref>{{cite web |title=Oral history interview with Alex Hershaft |url=https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/irn511491 |website=Holocaust Memorial Museum}}</ref> After recovering from a long illness, she opened a holistic health and nutrition wellness center in Los Angeles in 2008.<ref name=":1" /> She now resides and practices in Scottsdale, Arizona.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VRQTOlv8OzI&t|title=Stay Sick or Eat Meat? Facing a Vegan Crisis – Monica Hershaft – #897|website=[[YouTube]]|date=February 2022 }}</ref>

He currently resides in [[Bethesda, Maryland|Bethesda, MD]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Animal rights pioneer, a Holocaust survivor, encourages respect, obligation |url=https://jewishchronicle.timesofisrael.com/animal-rights-pioneer-a-holocaust-survivor-encourages-respect-obligation/ |website=jewishchronicle.timesofisrael.com |date=24 February 2025}}</ref>
Hershaft became a vegetarian in 1961 and a vegan in 1981. He has been physically active throughout his life, mostly by playing soccer on various school and county teams, running marathons in the 1980s and 1990s and more recently, by engaging in [[Folk dance|regular folk dancing]] and [[swimming]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vegetarians in Paradise/Alex Hershaft/FARM/24 Carrot Vegetarian Award |url=https://www.vegparadise.com/24carrot411.html |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=www.vegparadise.com}}</ref>
